title: Scientific Knowledge Types
purpose: Seed distinct scientific knowledge-object types so Lantern represents observations, measurements, hypotheses, regularities, laws, models and theories according to their epistemic roles rather than treating them as confidence levels on one ladder.

concepts.definition: A documented observation of a phenomenon/event/state under stated conditions; interpretation may be attached but remains distinguishable from the observation record.
A measurement record with quantity/value, units where applicable, uncertainty, method/instrument and scope.
A proposed, sufficiently specified claim/explanation/prediction that can be evaluated against possible evidence; hypotheses vary in support.
A recurring observed relationship/pattern within a stated scope, without necessarily supplying an explanation.

A compact descriptive generalization, often mathematical, representing a well-supported regularity under stated conditions/scope; a law primarily describes rather than serving as a confidence rank above theory.
A simplified formal/conceptual/computational representation used to describe, explain, predict or simulate aspects of a system under assumptions.
A broad explanatory framework integrating mechanisms/models/evidence and generating predictions across a domain; theory is not a lower-confidence precursor to law.
A stated expected observation/result derived from a hypothesis, model, theory or law under specified conditions.
A premise/condition accepted for a model or analysis; assumptions should be explicit because conclusions may depend on them.
A representation intentionally simplified and valid to a specified tolerance/scope.
A condition delimiting where a law/model/theory is intended or known to apply.
A reliable observation/result that is not adequately accounted for by the currently applied model/theory under expected scope.
Degree of convergence among relevant expert communities/evidence assessments; consensus is evidence about the state of inquiry, not a truth-maker.
Evidence-relative status such as candidate, supported, well-supported, contested, scope-limited, stale/review-due, superseded or historical.

guards.reason: Scientific theory names an explanatory object type, not a low-confidence status.
Theories and laws have different scientific roles; confidence does not convert one type into the other.
Law/theory type does not rank truth or confidence.
Observation records what occurred; explanation requires additional inference/model.
Models are representations with assumptions and scope.
Successful predictions support a theory/model but alternatives may also predict the result.
Check measurement, assumptions, auxiliary hypotheses and scope before global rejection.
Consensus summarizes expert/evidence convergence and can be wrong or revised.
Superseded models/theories may remain useful approximations within restricted scopes.
An anomaly motivates investigation; reliability, assumptions and scope require evaluation.

invariants: Scientific knowledge type and confidence/status are orthogonal.
Hypothesis, law and theory are not stages on a single maturity ladder.
Laws primarily describe regularities; theories primarily organize/explain/predict; models represent systems under assumptions.
Observations and measurements preserve their records separately from interpretations.
Predictions retain provenance to the hypothesis/model/theory/law that generated them.
Models/theories/laws carry scope, assumptions and boundary conditions where applicable.
Scientific consensus is represented as a state of expert/evidence convergence, not truth.
Anomalies trigger investigation rather than automatic rejection or suppression.
Supersession/refinement preserves belief genealogy and possible restricted usefulness.
Scientific objects never gain authority/permission merely from epistemic status.

provenance.authoring_basis: Philosophy and practice of science distinctions among observation, hypothesis, empirical regularity, law, model and theory, adapted to Lantern's typed epistemic architecture.
